summary: Paul turns from his story to the Galatians' own experience and then to Scripture: did they receive the Spirit by works of law or by hearing of faith? Abraham believed God and was counted righteous before circumcision existed; the promise came 430 years before the law and cannot be annulled by it. The law was a custodian for the period before Christ — and now that faith has come, the custodian is dismissed: in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female.
whyItMatters: This is the letter's courtroom: experience, then Genesis and Habakkuk, are called as witnesses that the promise — not the law — is the basis of belonging, and that the law had a defined and temporary assignment. Nearly every later Christian argument about law and faith runs through these twenty-nine verses.

context.author: Paul, arguing in the rhetorical mode of a cross-examination: the chapter asks the Galatians questions they must answer from their own experience before it turns to Scripture.
context.audience: Gentile believers in Galatia who received the Spirit when Paul preached, and are now being told to add law-keeping.
context.date: Undated within the letter; the argument turns on the 430-year gap between promise and law (3:17), not on the letter's own year.
context.setting: The situation of chapter 1: assemblies being persuaded to take on circumcision and calendar; this chapter is the theological core of the reply.
context.literaryForm: Argument by question-and-answer — the chapter's sentences are mostly questions until the Abraham argument begins — followed by a sustained chain of quoted Scripture with inference drawn at each link.

outline.heading: The experience questions
outline.note: Foolish Galatians: did you receive the Spirit by works of law or by hearing of faith? Did you begin in the Spirit to be completed in the flesh? The questions assume answers the readers already hold.

outline.heading: Abraham believed — and that was the count
outline.note: Genesis is quoted: Abraham 'believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness'; those of faith are his children, and Scripture foresaw the Gentiles' blessing, so those of faith are blessed with faithful Abraham.

outline.heading: The curse of relying on the law
outline.note: Those of works of law are under a curse, for the law itself requires doing all of it; 'The righteous will live by faith'; Christ redeemed us from the law's curse by becoming a curse — 'Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree' — so the blessing of Abraham could reach the nations.

outline.heading: The promise outranks the later law
outline.note: A confirmed human covenant is not annulled or added to; the promise spoke to Abraham and to one offspring — Christ — and the law, arriving 430 years later, cannot make the promise ineffective; the inheritance is by promise.

outline.heading: So why the law at all?
outline.note: Added because of transgressions until the offspring should come, ordained through angels by a mediator; the law is not against the promises — but it could not make alive, and Scripture imprisoned all under sin so the promise would be received by faith.

outline.heading: The custodian dismissed
outline.note: Before faith came they were kept in custody under the law, the tutor leading to Christ; now that faith has come the tutor is no longer needed — you are all children of God through faith, baptized into Christ, one in him, Abraham's offspring and heirs according to promise.

keyVerses.text: Even so, Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness.” Know therefore that those who are of faith are children of Abraham.
keyVerses.why: The pivot of the whole argument: Abraham's righteousness is dated by Scripture itself to belief, before circumcision or law existed — so the family is defined by faith, and Gentiles qualify.

keyVerses.text: So that the law has become our tutor to bring us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith. But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a tutor.
keyVerses.why: The chapter's answer to 'why the law at all': a paidagōgos — the custodian who escorted a minor — honored for its season and then set aside when the heir comes of age.

keyVerses.text: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus.
keyVerses.why: The letter's most quoted verse about who belongs: in the argument's own flow it states the make-up of the promise-defined family, with the divisions of the ancient world named and overridden.

themes: the Spirit received by hearing of faith
the promise 430 years before the law
the law as custodian until Christ

questions.question: Why does Paul call the Galatians foolish?
questions.answer: 'Foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you' (3:1) — the word targets one specific failure: they saw Christ 'openly portrayed among you as crucified' and are now turning from what they saw. The chapter immediately explains the charge with the experience questions: they began by the Spirit and are being told to continue by the flesh (3:3).

questions.question: What is the argument from the Spirit in verses 2-5?
questions.answer: Paul asks the Galatians to testify from their own experience: the Spirit came, and works of law had nothing to do with it — 'Did you receive the Spirit by the works of the law, or by hearing of faith?' The argument is that a new requirement cannot be added to a beginning it had no part in: having begun in the Spirit, they are not completed in the flesh.

questions.question: How does Abraham prove Paul's case?
questions.answer: Genesis is quoted saying Abraham 'believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness' (3:6). Chronology is the argument: circumcision had not been given and the law was 430 years away (3:17), so Abraham's standing with God — by belief — predates every boundary marker the agitators are demanding. Those of faith are therefore his children (3:7), and Scripture's promise that 'all the nations will be blessed' in him is the Gentile mission's own foundation (3:8).

questions.question: What is the curse of the law in verses 10-13?
questions.answer: Paul reads two Scripture quotes against each other: the law requires doing 'all things written in the book of the law' and pronounces a curse on anyone who does not continue in them, while 'The righteous will live by faith.' Reliance on law-keeping therefore means standing under a curse no one fully escapes — and Christ's death, 'having become a curse for us' by the Deuteronomy line 'Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree,' redeems from that curse so the blessing of Abraham can reach the nations (3:13-14).

questions.question: Does Paul say the law is against the promises of God?
questions.answer: He asks exactly that and answers 'Certainly not!' (3:21). The law's problem in this chapter is capacity, not character: no law was given that could 'make alive,' so righteousness was never going to come by it. Its assignment was different — added 'because of transgressions, until the offspring should come' (3:19).

questions.question: Why does Paul stress that the promise came 430 years before the law?
questions.answer: It is a priority argument: a covenant confirmed beforehand by God is not voided or amended by something added later — Paul argues this even from ordinary human covenants (3:15). Since the inheritance was granted 'by promise' (3:18), the law cannot convert it into a wage or an entry exam; the sequence itself protects the promise.

questions.question: What does the 'tutor' mean in verse 24?
questions.answer: The Greek paidagōgos was not a schoolteacher but the household custodian who escorted a child and kept discipline until the heir came of age. The image honors the law's assignment — real authority, for a defined period — and explains 'we are no longer under a tutor' (3:25) as the coming of age Paul described in 3:23: the period has an end, and the end is faith's arrival.

questions.question: Why are angels and a mediator mentioned in verse 19-20?
questions.answer: Paul notes the law 'was ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator' — details that mark it as different in kind from the direct promise to Abraham. The next verse, 'a mediator is not between one, but God is one,' is one of the letter's most compressed and argued-over sentences; readers differ on its exact force, and the safest reading stays with the contrast the chapter is drawing: the promise came directly, the law through intermediaries.

questions.question: What does 3:28 mean by 'neither Jew nor Greek'?
questions.answer: In the chapter's own flow the verse states the composition of the promise-family: those baptized into Christ have 'put on Christ,' and the ancient world's three deep divisions — ethnicity, status, and sex — do not define standing in him. The letter's argument here is about who belongs to Abraham's family by promise; later readers have carried the principle into social questions in more than one direction, and those extensions are exactly that — extensions beyond the verse's own claim.

glossary.def: The hosted text's word for paidagōgos — the household custodian who escorted and disciplined a minor until the heir came of age; Paul's image for the law's temporary assignment (3:24).
The word the promise uses of Abraham's line; Paul notes it is singular — 'to your offspring, which is Christ' (3:16) — before declaring all who belong to Christ are that offspring (3:29).
Paul's image for the period before faith: 'we were kept in custody under the law, confined for the faith which should afterwards be revealed' (3:23).
